statement: If $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ is open and $f\colon U \to \mathbb{R}^n$ is a [smooth map](c:smooth-map), then the set of [critical values](c:critical-value) of $f$ has [measure zero](c:measure-zero) in $\mathbb{R}^n$.

hypotheses.text: The domain $U$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^m$.
The map $f\colon U \to \mathbb{R}^n$ is [smooth](c:smooth-map), that is, of class $C^\infty$.

conclusion: The image $f(C)$ of the set $C$ of [critical points](c:critical-point) has Lebesgue measure zero.

proofs.name: Induction on dimension with slicing
proofs.slogan: Filter the critical points by vanishing derivatives, slice the first pieces by induction and Fubini, and crush the last piece with Taylor estimates.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, by induction on $m$; for $m = 0$ the image is at most one point. The version for second countable manifolds follows by countably many charts.

roles.why: Openness gives room for local changes of coordinates and a countable cover of $U$ by small neighborhoods.
Smoothness supplies derivatives of every order, so the filtration never stops and Taylor's theorem applies to every order.

steps.slogan: Filter the critical set by the order of the vanishing partial derivatives.
steps.detail: Let $C$ be the set of [critical points](c:critical-point), where $df_x$ has rank less than $n$, and let $C_i$ be the set where all partial derivatives of order $1$ to $i$ vanish. Then $C \supseteq C_1 \supseteq C_2 \supseteq \cdots$, and the claim follows if each piece $C \setminus C_1$, $C_k \setminus C_{k+1}$ and $C_K$ has an image of measure zero.

steps.slogan: Straighten one coordinate near $C \setminus C_1$ and slice the image into hyperplanes.
steps.detail: Near $x \in C \setminus C_1$ some $\partial f_1/\partial x_1 \neq 0$, so $h(x) = (f_1(x), x_2, \dots, x_m)$ is a local [diffeomorphism](c:diffeomorph) and $g = f \circ h^{-1}$ keeps each hyperplane $x_1 = t$. Critical points of $g$ are critical for its slices, so induction makes every slice of critical values null, and Fubini's theorem makes the whole set null.

steps.slogan: Push $C_k \setminus C_{k+1}$ into a hyperplane and apply the induction hypothesis there.
steps.detail: Near $x \in C_k \setminus C_{k+1}$ some $k$-th derivative $w$ has $\partial w/\partial x_1 \neq 0$, so $h(x) = (w(x), x_2, \dots, x_m)$ is a local diffeomorphism that sends $C_k$ into the hyperplane $x_1 = 0$. These points are critical for $f \circ h^{-1}$ on that hyperplane, so induction makes their image null.

steps.slogan: Bound the image of $C_K$ on small cubes by Taylor's theorem when $K > m/n - 1$.
steps.detail: On a cube of side $\delta$, Taylor's theorem gives $|f(x + y) - f(x)| \le c|y|^{K+1}$ for $x \in C_K$. Split the cube into $r^m$ cubes of side $\delta/r$; each one that meets $C_K$ has image in a cube of side $a/r^{K+1}$, so the image has outer measure at most $r^m a^n r^{-n(K+1)} \to 0$, because $n(K+1) > m$.

steps.slogan: Cover the critical set by countably many pieces and add their null images.
steps.detail: Each piece is covered by countably many of the neighborhoods of steps 2 to 4, because $U$ is second countable. So $f(C)$ is a countable union of sets of [measure zero](c:measure-zero) for [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure), and it has measure zero.

concepts.c:smooth-map: Smoothness gives the derivatives of every order that the filtration needs.
concepts.c:critical-value: The theorem bounds the size of the set of critical values.
concepts.c:measure-zero: Each piece of the critical set has an image of measure zero.
concepts.c:critical-point: Critical points are split into pieces by the order of vanishing derivatives.
concepts.c:diffeomorph: Local diffeomorphisms straighten one coordinate so that slicing is possible.
concepts.c:lebesgue-measure: Null sets for Lebesgue measure are closed under countable unions.

statement: If $A$ and $B$ are [positive-definite](c:positive-definite-matrix) $n \times n$ matrices over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, then their [Hadamard product](c:hadamard-product) $A \circ B$, with entries $a_{ij} b_{ij}$, is positive definite.

hypotheses.text: The matrix $A$ is Hermitian and [positive definite](c:positive-definite-matrix): $x^* A x > 0$ for $x \neq 0$.
The matrix $B$ is Hermitian and positive definite.

conclusion: The matrix $A \circ B$ is Hermitian and $x^*(A \circ B)x > 0$ for every $x \neq 0$.

formal.difference: The declaration allows any index type, with finitely supported test vectors, over any field of type RCLike. For a finite index set it states the same.

proofs.name: Kronecker product on diagonal vectors
proofs.slogan: Write the quadratic form of $A \circ B$ as the quadratic form of the positive-definite Kronecker product on a diagonal vector.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for $n \ge 1$; for $n = 0$ there is no nonzero vector and the claim is empty.

roles.why: $A$ is Hermitian, and it factors as $C^* C$ with $C$ invertible.
$B$ is Hermitian, and it factors as $D^* D$ with $D$ invertible.

steps.slogan: Check that the entrywise product of two Hermitian matrices is Hermitian.
steps.detail: The conjugate of $a_{ji} b_{ji}$ is $\overline{a_{ji}}\,\overline{b_{ji}} = a_{ij} b_{ij}$, so $(A \circ B)^* = A \circ B$.

steps.slogan: Factor $A$ and $B$ to show that the [Kronecker product](c:kronecker-product) $A \otimes B$ is positive definite.
steps.detail: Write $A = C^* C$ and $B = D^* D$ with $C$ and $D$ invertible, for example the positive square roots. The mixed-product rule gives $A \otimes B = (C \otimes D)^*(C \otimes D)$, and $C \otimes D$ is invertible, so $v^*(A \otimes B)v = \|(C \otimes D)v\|^2 > 0$ for $v \neq 0$.

steps.slogan: Embed the test vector $x$ as the diagonal vector $v$ with $v_{(i,k)} = x_i \delta_{ik}$.
steps.detail: Since $(A \otimes B)_{(i,k),(j,l)} = a_{ij} b_{kl}$, only the terms with $k = i$ and $l = j$ survive in $v^*(A \otimes B)v$. So $v^*(A \otimes B)v = \sum_{i,j} \overline{x_i} a_{ij} b_{ij} x_j = x^*(A \circ B)x$, and $v \neq 0$ when $x \neq 0$.

steps.slogan: Combine the identity with step 2 to get $x^*(A \circ B)x > 0$.
steps.detail: For $x \neq 0$, steps 2 and 3 give $x^*(A \circ B)x = v^*(A \otimes B)v > 0$. With step 1, $A \circ B$ is a Hermitian [positive-definite matrix](c:positive-definite-matrix).

concepts.c:positive-definite-matrix: Positive definiteness is assumed for both factors and proved for the product.
concepts.c:hadamard-product: The Hadamard product is the matrix whose quadratic form the proof controls.
concepts.c:kronecker-product: The Kronecker product carries the positivity, and the Hadamard product sits inside it.

proofs.name: Spectral decomposition of one factor
proofs.slogan: Decompose $B$ into rank-one pieces by the spectral theorem and write $A \circ B$ as a positive sum of congruent copies of $A$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for $n \ge 1$; the same argument shows that the product of two positive semidefinite matrices is positive semidefinite.

roles.why: Positivity of $A$ makes each term $y^* A y$ nonnegative and positive for $y \neq 0$.
$B$ is Hermitian with positive [eigenvalues](c:eigenvalue), so the spectral theorem applies.

steps.slogan: Write $B = \sum_k \mu_k u_k u_k^*$ with positive eigenvalues and orthonormal eigenvectors.
steps.detail: The spectral theorem gives an orthonormal basis of [eigenvectors](c:eigenvector) $u_1, \dots, u_n$ of the Hermitian matrix $B$ with eigenvalues $\mu_k$, and $\mu_k > 0$ because $B$ is positive definite.

steps.slogan: Show that $A \circ (u u^*) = D_u A D_u^*$ with $D_u = \mathrm{diag}(u)$.
steps.detail: Both matrices have entries $u_i a_{ij} \overline{u_j}$. So $x^*(A \circ uu^*)x = y^* A y$ with $y = D_u^* x$, which is at least $0$; this makes each piece a [positive semidefinite matrix](c:positive-semidefinite-matrix).

steps.slogan: Expand the quadratic form of $A \circ B$ as a sum of nonnegative terms.
steps.detail: The Hadamard product is linear in $B$, so $x^*(A \circ B)x = \sum_k \mu_k\, y_k^* A y_k$ with $y_k = D_{u_k}^* x$, and every term is at least $0$ by step 2.

steps.slogan: Find one term with $y_k \neq 0$ to get strict positivity.
steps.detail:
Let $x_i 
eq 0$. The rows of the unitary matrix with columns $u_k$ have norm $1$, so $u_k(i) 
eq 0$ for some $k$; then $y_k$ has entry $\overline{u_k(i)} x_i 
eq 0$ and $\mu_k y_k^* A y_k > 0$. Hence $x^*(A \circ B)x > 0$.

concepts.c:positive-definite-matrix: Positive definiteness of $A$ gives the strict sign of each term.
concepts.c:hadamard-product: The Hadamard product is linear in $B$, so the spectral sum passes through it.
concepts.c:eigenvalue: Positive eigenvalues of $B$ weight the sum with positive coefficients.
concepts.c:eigenvector: Orthonormal eigenvectors split $B$ into rank-one pieces.
concepts.c:positive-semidefinite-matrix: Each rank-one piece gives a positive semidefinite congruent copy of $A$.

statement: Let $X$ be a [compact space](c:compact-space) and $A$ a [subalgebra](c:subalgebra) of $C(X, \mathbb{R})$ that contains the constants and separates points. Then $A$ is [dense](c:dense-set) in $C(X, \mathbb{R})$: every [continuous](c:continuous-function) $f\colon X \to \mathbb{R}$ is a [uniform limit](c:uniform-convergence) of functions in $A$.

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is [compact](c:compact-space).
$A$ is a [subalgebra](c:subalgebra) of $C(X, \mathbb{R})$ that contains the constant functions.
$A$ separates points: for $x \neq y$ some $g \in A$ has $g(x) \neq g(y)$.

conclusion: The closure of $A$ for the supremum norm is all of $C(X, \mathbb{R})$.

proofs.name: Closed sublattice and two finite subcovers
proofs.slogan: Show that the closure of $A$ is a lattice that interpolates at any two points, then glue interpolants by two finite subcovers.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; for empty $X$ the claim is trivial. A point-separating family of continuous functions makes $X$ a [Hausdorff space](c:hausdorff-space), so no separation axiom is assumed.

roles.why: Compactness makes the supremum norm finite and reduces the two open covers to finite subcovers.
Sums, products and constants put polynomials in $f$ and affine changes of $g$ into $A$.
A separating function makes the two-point interpolation possible.

steps.slogan: Pass to the closure $L$ of $A$, a closed subalgebra with the same properties.
steps.detail: Addition, multiplication and scalar multiplication are continuous for the supremum norm, so the closure $L$ of $A$ is again a [subalgebra](c:subalgebra). It contains the constants and separates points, and it suffices to show $L = C(X, \mathbb{R})$.

steps.slogan: Approximate $|t|$ by [polynomials](c:polynomial) to show that $|f| \in L$ for $f \in L$.
steps.detail: The values of $f$ lie in $[-\|f\|, \|f\|]$, where the Weierstrass approximation theorem gives polynomials $p_k \to |t|$ uniformly. Then $p_k \circ f \in L$ and $p_k \circ f \to |f|$ uniformly, so $|f| \in L$ because $L$ is closed.

steps.slogan: Express the maximum and the minimum of two functions by absolute values.
steps.detail: For $f, g \in L$, $\max(f, g) = (f + g + |f - g|)/2$ and $\min(f, g) = (f + g - |f - g|)/2$, so step 2 puts both in $L$. Thus $L$ is a lattice of functions.

steps.slogan: Interpolate any two values at any two points by a function of $L$.
steps.detail: For $x \neq y$ and reals $a, b$, choose $g \in A$ with $g(x) \neq g(y)$ and set $h = a + (b - a)(g - g(x))/(g(y) - g(x))$. Then $h \in L$, $h(x) = a$ and $h(y) = b$; for $x = y$ a constant works.

steps.slogan: Glue the interpolants by a minimum and a maximum over two finite subcovers.
steps.detail: Fix $f$, $\varepsilon > 0$ and $x$. Interpolants $h_{x,y}$ equal to $f$ at $x$ and $y$ satisfy $h_{x,y} < f + \varepsilon$ near $y$, so a finite subcover gives $g_x = \min_j h_{x,y_j} \in L$ with $g_x < f + \varepsilon$ and $g_x(x) = f(x)$. A second finite subcover gives $g = \max_i g_{x_i}$ with $|g - f| < \varepsilon$, so $f \in L$.

concepts.c:compact-space: Compactness turns the two open covers into finite subcovers.
concepts.c:subalgebra: Closure under algebra operations lets polynomials in $f$ stay in $A$.
concepts.c:dense-set: Density is the conclusion: the closure of $A$ is everything.
concepts.c:continuous-function: The target functions and the approximants are continuous real functions.
concepts.c:uniform-convergence: Approximation is measured in the supremum norm, so limits are uniform.
concepts.c:hausdorff-space: Point separation already forces the Hausdorff property, so it is not assumed.
concepts.c:polynomial: Polynomials approximating $|t|$ bring absolute values into the closure.

statement: For every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $\delta > 0$ such that every [graph](c:graph) on $n$ vertices with fewer than $\delta n^3$ triangles has a [triangle-free](c:triangle-free-graph) [subgraph](c:is-subgraph) obtained by removing fewer than $\varepsilon n^2$ edges.

hypotheses.text: The tolerance satisfies $\varepsilon > 0$.
The [graph](c:graph) $G$ on $n$ vertices has fewer than $\delta n^3$ triangles, where $\delta = \delta(\varepsilon)$ is the constant of the lemma.

conclusion: Removing fewer than $\varepsilon n^2$ edges of $G$ leaves a triangle-free graph.

formal.difference: The declaration fixes $\delta$ as the explicit tower-type constant triangleRemovalBound ε and counts triangles as 3-cliques. Otherwise it states the same.

proofs.name: Regularity partition and triangle counting
proofs.slogan: Assume that the graph is far from triangle-free, clean it with a regularity partition, and count the triangles that a surviving triangle forces.
proofs.scope: The contrapositive: a graph that needs at least $\varepsilon n^2$ deletions has at least $\delta n^3$ triangles. Small graphs with $n \le \lceil 4/\varepsilon \rceil$ are a separate case.

roles.why: A positive $\varepsilon$ fixes the regularity parameter $\varepsilon/8$ and the threshold $\lceil 4/\varepsilon \rceil$.
The forced count of at least $\delta n^3$ triangles contradicts this hypothesis.

steps.slogan: Assume that every triangle-free subgraph misses at least $\varepsilon n^2$ edges of $G$.
steps.detail: Argue by contraposition: suppose no removal of fewer than $\varepsilon n^2$ edges makes $G$ [triangle-free](c:triangle-free-graph). The goal is at least $\delta n^3$ triangles, with $\delta$ depending only on $\varepsilon$.

steps.slogan: Treat the graphs with at most $\lceil 4/\varepsilon \rceil$ vertices by one triangle.
steps.detail: Since $G$ itself is not triangle-free, it has at least one triangle. The constant $\delta$ is chosen with $\delta l^3 \le 1$ for $l = \lceil 4/\varepsilon \rceil$, so for $n \le l$ the bound $\delta n^3$ is at most $1$, which is at most the number of triangles.

steps.slogan: Apply the regularity lemma with parameter $\varepsilon/8$ to the large graph.
steps.detail: For $n > l$, Szemerédi's regularity lemma gives an equipartition of the vertices into $k$ parts, $l \le k \le M$ with $M$ depending only on $\varepsilon$, in which all but an $\varepsilon/8$ fraction of the pairs of parts are [regular](c:epsilon-regular-pair) with parameter $\varepsilon/8$.

steps.slogan: Delete the edges inside parts, in irregular pairs and in sparse pairs.
steps.detail: Edges inside parts number at most $n^2/k \le \varepsilon n^2/4$. Edges in irregular pairs and edges in pairs of density below $\varepsilon/4$ number at most $\varepsilon n^2/4$ each, up to rounding. So the reduced [subgraph](c:is-subgraph) $G'$ loses fewer than $\varepsilon n^2$ edges.

steps.slogan: Find a triangle of $G'$ across three regular pairs of density at least $\varepsilon/4$.
steps.detail: By step 1, $G'$ still has a triangle $xyz$. Its vertices lie in three different parts $X, Y, Z$, and each pair among them is $\varepsilon/8$-regular with density at least $\varepsilon/4$, because all other edges were deleted.

steps.slogan: Count the triangles across $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ with the triangle counting lemma.
steps.detail: The triangle counting lemma gives at least $c(\varepsilon)|X||Y||Z|$ triangles in $G$, and each part has at least $n/(2M)$ vertices. This is at least $\delta n^3$ triangles, which contradicts the hypothesis.

concepts.c:graph: The lemma is a statement about finite simple graphs and their edges.
concepts.c:triangle-free-graph: The goal is a triangle-free subgraph after few deletions.
concepts.c:is-subgraph: The reduced graph is a subgraph of $G$ with few edges removed.
concepts.c:epsilon-regular-pair: Regular pairs behave like random graphs, so they carry many triangles.

statement: Let $r \ge 1$. A [graph](c:graph) on $n$ vertices with no [clique](c:clique) of $r + 1$ vertices has at most as many edges as the [Turán graph](c:turan-graph) $T(n, r)$, and it has exactly as many if and only if it is isomorphic to $T(n, r)$.

hypotheses.text: The integer $r$ satisfies $r \ge 1$.
The [graph](c:graph) $G$ on $n$ vertices has no [clique](c:clique) of $r + 1$ vertices.

conclusion: $e(G) \le e(T(n, r))$, with equality exactly when $G \cong T(n, r)$, the complete $r$-partite graph with part sizes $\lfloor n/r \rfloor$ or $\lceil n/r \rceil$.

formal.difference: The declaration states that a clique-free graph with the most edges is exactly a graph isomorphic to $T(n, r)$. The edge bound follows at once because such a maximal graph exists.

proofs.name: Zykov symmetrization
proofs.slogan: In an edge-maximal clique-free graph, copy vertices to show that non-adjacency is an equivalence with balanced classes.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; for $n \le r$ the Turán graph is the complete graph $K_n$. The case $n = 0$ is trivial.

roles.why: With $r \ge 1$ the empty graph is clique-free and $T(n, r)$ is defined.
Copying a vertex keeps the graph clique-free, and one vertex per class forms a clique.

steps.slogan: Choose a clique-free graph with the most edges on the $n$ vertices.
steps.detail: There are finitely many graphs on $n$ vertices, and the empty graph has no clique of $r + 1 \ge 2$ vertices. So a maximal graph $G_0$ exists.

steps.slogan: Show that nonadjacent vertices of a maximal graph have equal [degree](c:vertex-degree).
steps.detail: If $s \not\sim t$ and $\deg t < \deg s$, give $t$ the neighbors of $s$. A clique through the new $t$ misses $s$, so it gives a clique in the old graph, and the edge count grows by $\deg s - \deg t > 0$, which contradicts maximality.

steps.slogan: Show that non-adjacency is transitive in a maximal graph.
steps.detail: If $t \not\sim s$, $s \not\sim u$ but $t \sim u$, replace $t$ and $u$ by copies of $s$. The graph stays clique-free, and by step 2 the edge count changes by $2\deg s - (\deg t + \deg u - 1) = 1 > 0$, a contradiction.

steps.slogan: Read the maximal graph as complete multipartite with at most $r$ parts.
steps.detail: The classes of non-adjacency are independent sets, and vertices in different classes are adjacent. One vertex from each class forms a [clique](c:clique), so there are at most $r$ classes.

steps.slogan: Move single vertices to show that the parts are balanced and number $\min(n, r)$.
steps.detail: If $|P| \ge |Q| + 2$, moving one vertex from $P$ to $Q$ adds $|P| - 1 - |Q| > 0$ edges. If there are fewer than $\min(n, r)$ parts, splitting one vertex off a part of size at least $2$ adds edges. So the maximal graph is isomorphic to $T(n, r)$.

steps.slogan: Compare every clique-free graph with the maximal graph $T(n, r)$.
steps.detail: $T(n, r)$ has no $(r + 1)$-clique, since two of its vertices would share a part. By steps 1 to 5 the maximum edge count equals $e(T(n, r))$, so $e(G) \le e(T(n, r))$, and equality makes $G$ maximal, hence isomorphic to $T(n, r)$.

concepts.c:graph: The theorem compares edge counts of graphs on a fixed vertex set.
concepts.c:clique: Cliques are the forbidden subgraphs, and copying vertices never creates them.
concepts.c:turan-graph: The Turán graph is the unique extremal graph that the proof reaches.
concepts.c:vertex-degree: Equal degrees make the vertex copying in step 3 gain exactly one edge.

statement: In a [normal space](c:normal-space) $X$, for any two disjoint [closed sets](c:closed-set) $A$ and $B$ there is a [continuous function](c:continuous-function) $f\colon X \to [0, 1]$ with $f = 0$ on $A$ and $f = 1$ on $B$.

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is [normal](c:normal-space): disjoint closed sets have disjoint open neighborhoods.
The sets $A$ and $B$ are [closed](c:closed-set) in $X$.
The sets $A$ and $B$ are disjoint.

conclusion: Some continuous $f\colon X \to \mathbb{R}$ has values in $[0, 1]$, equals $0$ on $A$ and equals $1$ on $B$.

proofs.name: Averaged approximations
proofs.slogan: Split each closed-open pair by normality, average indicator functions along the splittings, and show that the limit varies by at most $(3/4)^n$ near each point.
proofs.scope: The whole lemma. The construction works for every pair $(C, U)$ of a closed set inside an open set, and the lemma uses the pair $(A, X \setminus B)$.

roles.why: Normality gives an open set with its [closure](c:closure) between a closed set and an open superset.
$A$ is closed and $X \setminus B$ is open, so $(A, X \setminus B)$ is a valid starting pair.
Disjointness gives $A \subseteq X \setminus B$.

steps.slogan: Split a closed set $C$ inside an open set $U$ by an open set $V$ with $\overline{V} \subseteq U$.
steps.detail: Normality separates $C$ from the closed set $X \setminus U$, which gives an open $V$ with $C \subseteq V \subseteq \overline{V} \subseteq U$. The pair $(C, U)$ splits into a left pair $(C, V)$ and a right pair $(\overline{V}, U)$.

steps.slogan: Define approximations recursively as averages of the left and right approximations.
steps.detail: For a pair $c = (C, U)$ let $a_0(c)$ be the indicator of $X \setminus U$ and $a_{n+1}(c) = (a_n(\text{left}) + a_n(\text{right}))/2$. By induction each $a_n(c)$ has values in $[0, 1]$, is $0$ on $C$, is $1$ outside $U$, and increases with $n$.

steps.slogan: Take the pointwise limit of the increasing bounded approximations.
steps.detail: The limit $f_c = \lim_n a_n(c)$ exists, has values in $[0, 1]$, is $0$ on $C$ and $1$ outside $U$. It satisfies $f_c = (f_{\text{left}} + f_{\text{right}})/2$.

steps.slogan: Show by induction on $n$ that $f_c$ varies by at most $(3/4)^n$ near each point.
steps.detail: If $x \in V$, then near $x$ the right function is $0$ and the left one varies by at most $(3/4)^n$, so $f_c$ varies by at most $(3/4)^n/2$. Otherwise the left-left function is $1$ near $x$, and the recurrence with the triangle inequality gives $(3/4)^{n+1}$. So $f_c$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function).

steps.slogan: Apply the construction to the pair $(A, X \setminus B)$.
steps.detail: The set $A$ is closed, $X \setminus B$ is [open](c:open-set), and $A \subseteq X \setminus B$ by disjointness. The function $f = f_{(A, X \setminus B)}$ is continuous with values in $[0, 1]$, equals $0$ on $A$ and equals $1$ on $B$.

concepts.c:normal-space: Normality is the only tool that produces the intermediate open sets.
concepts.c:closed-set: The closed set $A$ starts the first closed-open pair.
concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity of the limit is the hard part of the construction.
concepts.c:closure: Closures of the new open sets become the closed sets of right pairs.
concepts.c:open-set: The complement of $B$ is the open set of the first pair.

proofs.name: Open sets indexed by dyadic rationals
proofs.slogan: Build nested open sets indexed by dyadic rationals and let $f(x)$ be the least index of a set that contains $x$.
proofs.scope: The whole lemma, by the classical construction; the case $A = \emptyset$ or $B = \emptyset$ needs no change.

roles.why: Normality inserts a new open set between any two nested ones.
$X \setminus B$ is open and $A$ is closed, so they start the nested family.
Disjointness gives $A \subseteq X \setminus B$, so $f = 0$ on $A$ and $f = 1$ on $B$.

steps.slogan: Build open sets $U_r$ for [dyadic rationals](c:dyadic-rational-number) $r \in [0, 1]$ with $\overline{U_r} \subseteq U_s$ for $r < s$.
steps.detail: Set $U_1 = X \setminus B$ and choose open $U_0$ with $A \subseteq U_0 \subseteq \overline{U_0} \subseteq U_1$ by normality. If $U_r$ is built for all dyadics with denominator $2^k$, normality inserts $U_t$ with $\overline{U_r} \subseteq U_t \subseteq \overline{U_t} \subseteq U_s$ between consecutive ones.

steps.slogan: Define $f(x)$ as the infimum of the indices $r$ with $x \in U_r$.
steps.detail: Let $f(x) = \inf\{r : x \in U_r\}$, with $f(x) = 1$ when no $U_r$ contains $x$. Then $f$ has values in $[0, 1]$, $f = 0$ on $A \subseteq U_0$, and $f = 1$ on $B$, which meets no $U_r$.

steps.slogan: Relate the values of $f$ to the sets $\overline{U_r}$ and $U_r$.
steps.detail: If $x \in \overline{U_r}$, then $x \in U_s$ for every dyadic $s > r$, so $f(x) \le r$. If $x \notin U_r$, then $x \notin U_s$ for $s < r$, so $f(x) \ge r$.

steps.slogan: Trap $f$ on the open set $U_s \setminus \overline{U_r}$ to prove continuity.
steps.detail: If $f(x) \in (a, b)$, choose dyadics $r < s$ with $a < r < f(x) < s < b$, adjusting at the ends $0$ and $1$. Step 3 puts $x$ in the open set $W = U_s \setminus \overline{U_r}$ and gives $f(W) \subseteq [r, s] \subseteq (a, b)$, so $f$ is continuous.

concepts.c:normal-space: Normality inserts each new open set of the dyadic family.
concepts.c:closed-set: The closed set $A$ sits inside the first open set $U_0$.
concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity follows by trapping $f$ between two dyadic levels.
concepts.c:dyadic-rational-number: Dyadic rationals are dense and can be built by repeated halving.
concepts.c:closure: The closures $\overline{U_r}$ control the values of $f$ from above.

source.note: The classical dyadic proof, as in J. R. Munkres, Topology, theorem 33.1; not the mathlib route.

statement: If $\sum |a_n|$ converges for real or complex numbers $a_n$, then the [series](c:series) $\sum a_n$ converges, $|\sum a_n| \le \sum |a_n|$, and every rearrangement $\sum a_{\sigma(n)}$ converges to the same sum.

hypotheses.text: The series $\sum |a_n|$ of real or complex numbers converges: $\sum a_n$ has [absolute convergence](c:absolute-convergence).

conclusion: $\sum a_n$ converges to some $S$ with $|S| \le \sum |a_n|$, and $\sum a_{\sigma(n)} = S$ for every bijection $\sigma$ of $\mathbb{N}$.

proofs.name: Cauchy criterion and small tails
proofs.slogan: Bound blocks of the series by blocks of absolute values, use completeness, and control rearrangements by one small tail.
proofs.scope: Real and complex series; the same proof works in every complete normed space.

roles.why: Convergence of $\sum |a_n|$ makes its blocks and tails small.

steps.slogan: Make the blocks and tails of $\sum |a_n|$ small.
steps.detail: The [partial sums](c:partial-sum) of the convergent series $\sum |a_n|$ form a [Cauchy sequence](c:cauchy-sequence). So for $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $N$ with $\sum_{n > N} |a_n| < \varepsilon$, and every block $\sum_{n=m+1}^{k} |a_n|$ with $k > m \ge N$ is below $\varepsilon$.

steps.slogan: Bound each block of $\sum a_n$ by the matching block of absolute values.
steps.detail: The triangle inequality gives $|S_k - S_m| = |\sum_{n=m+1}^{k} a_n| \le \sum_{n=m+1}^{k} |a_n| < \varepsilon$ for $k > m \ge N$. So the partial sums $S_k$ of $\sum a_n$ form a Cauchy sequence.

steps.slogan: Take the limit $S$ of the partial sums and bound it.
steps.detail: The [real numbers](c:real-number) and the complex numbers are complete, so $S_k \to S$. Since $|S_k| \le \sum_{n \le k} |a_n| \le \sum |a_n|$ for every $k$, the limit gives $|S| \le \sum |a_n|$.

steps.slogan: Compare a rearranged partial sum with $S_N$ through the small tail.
steps.detail: Choose $M$ with $\sigma(\{1, \dots, M\}) \supseteq \{1, \dots, N\}$. For $K \ge M$, the sum $\sum_{j \le K} a_{\sigma(j)} - S_N$ consists of terms $a_n$ with $n > N$, so its modulus is below $\varepsilon$, and $|S_N - S| \le \varepsilon$. Hence the rearranged sums converge to $S$.

concepts.c:series: The theorem concerns convergence of the series and of its rearrangements.
concepts.c:absolute-convergence: Absolute convergence is the hypothesis that makes all blocks small.
concepts.c:partial-sum: Convergence of a series means convergence of its partial sums.
concepts.c:cauchy-sequence: The Cauchy property passes from absolute values to the terms.
concepts.c:real-number: Completeness of the reals turns the Cauchy sequence into a limit.

source.note: The standard proof by the Cauchy criterion and a tail estimate, as in W. Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, theorems 3.45 and 3.55.

statement: In a [Banach space](c:banach-space) $E$, if a sequence $(x_n)$ satisfies $\sum \|x_n\| < \infty$, then the [series](c:series) $\sum x_n$ converges in $E$.

hypotheses.text: The space $E$ is a [Banach space](c:banach-space): a complete normed space.
The real series $\sum \|x_n\|$ of [norms](c:norm) converges.

conclusion: The partial sums $\sum_{n \le N} x_n$ converge in $E$.

formal.difference: The declaration proves unconditional summability over an arbitrary index type in a complete seminormed group. For the index set $\mathbb{N}$ this gives convergence of the partial sums, in every order.

proofs.name: Cauchy net of finite partial sums
proofs.slogan: Bound every finite sum far out by the matching sum of norms, so the partial sums are Cauchy, and take the limit by completeness.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; the argument is the same for any index set.

roles.why: Completeness turns the Cauchy partial sums into a limit.
Convergence of $\sum \|x_n\|$ makes the sums of norms far out small.

steps.slogan: Find $N$ such that every finite sum of norms beyond $N$ is below $\varepsilon$.
steps.detail: The real series $\sum \|x_n\|$ converges, so its partial sums form a [Cauchy sequence](c:cauchy-sequence). Hence for $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $N$ with $\sum_{n \in s} \|x_n\| < \varepsilon$ for every finite set $s$ of indices larger than $N$.

steps.slogan: Bound the norm of each finite sum by the sum of the [norms](c:norm).
steps.detail: The triangle inequality of the norm gives $\|\sum_{n \in s} x_n\| \le \sum_{n \in s} \|x_n\|$ for every finite set $s$. With step 1, every finite sum beyond $N$ has norm below $\varepsilon$.

steps.slogan: Show that the partial sums of $\sum x_n$ form a Cauchy sequence.
steps.detail: For $k > m \ge N$, the difference of the partial sums up to $k$ and up to $m$ is the finite sum over $\{m+1, \dots, k\}$, so its norm is below $\varepsilon$ by step 2.

steps.slogan: Take the limit of the Cauchy partial sums in the complete space $E$.
steps.detail: $E$ is a [Banach space](c:banach-space), so the Cauchy sequence of partial sums has a limit $x \in E$, and $\sum x_n = x$.

concepts.c:banach-space: Completeness of the normed space supplies the limit of the series.
concepts.c:series: The theorem gives convergence of the vector series $\sum x_n$.
concepts.c:norm: The norm's triangle inequality compares the vector sums with real sums.
concepts.c:cauchy-sequence: The Cauchy property passes from the real series to the vector series.

source.note: mathlib applies Summable.of_norm_bounded, which rewrites with summable_iff_cauchySeq_finset and uses cauchySeq_finset_of_norm_bounded.

statement: Let $L/K$ be a finite [abelian extension](c:abelian-extension) of number fields with [Galois group](c:galois-group) $G$, and let $C_K$ be the [idele class group](c:idele-class-group) of $K$. The [Artin map](c:artin-map) induces an isomorphism $C_K / N_{L/K}(C_L) \cong G$ that sends a uniformizer at each unramified prime $\mathfrak{p}$ to the [Frobenius element](c:frobenius-element) of $\mathfrak{p}$.

hypotheses.text: The extension $L/K$ of number fields is finite, Galois and [abelian](c:abelian-extension).

conclusion: The Artin map gives an isomorphism $C_K / N_{L/K}(C_L) \to \mathrm{Gal}(L/K)$, with Frobenius elements as the images of unramified primes.

proofs.name: The two inequalities and the reciprocity law
proofs.slogan: Glue the local reciprocity maps, prove the two index inequalities for the idele class group, and show that principal ideles map to the identity.
proofs.scope: An outline of the classical proof of global class field theory; every step rests on the cited book. The same outline works for global function fields.

roles.why: For an abelian extension the Frobenius elements and the local maps land in one abelian group $G$, and cyclic layers exist.

steps.slogan: Glue the local reciprocity maps into a homomorphism from the ideles of $K$ to $G$.
steps.detail: Local class field theory gives, for each place $v$, a map $K_v^\times \to \mathrm{Gal}(L_w/K_v) \subseteq G$ with kernel the local norms, sending a uniformizer at an unramified place to Frobenius. Their product is a continuous homomorphism on the ideles that kills the [norm map](c:norm-map) image of the ideles of $L$.

steps.slogan: Prove the first inequality with the Herbrand quotient of the idele class group.
steps.detail: For cyclic $L/K$, the Herbrand quotient of $C_L$ equals $[L : K]$, computed from the [local fields](c:local-field) and Dirichlet's unit theorem. Hence $[C_K : N_{L/K} C_L] \ge [L : K]$ for cyclic extensions.

steps.slogan: Prove the second inequality $[C_K : N_{L/K} C_L] \le [L : K]$ for every Galois extension.
steps.detail: An analytic proof uses Dirichlet $L$-series and the density of primes that split completely; an algebraic proof uses Kummer theory and Hilbert's theorem 90. With step 2, equality holds for cyclic extensions.

steps.slogan: Show that the glued map kills the principal ideles by reduction to cyclotomic fields.
steps.detail: For a cyclotomic extension of $\mathbb{Q}$ the Frobenius element of $p$ is $p$ modulo the conductor, and a direct computation shows that $K^\times$ maps to the identity. A general cyclic extension reduces to this case by a suitable cyclotomic base change, so the map factors through $C_K$.

steps.slogan: Compare indices to show that $C_K / N_{L/K} C_L \to G$ is an isomorphism.
steps.detail: The image fixes a subfield in which almost all primes split completely, and the second inequality forces that subfield to be $K$, so the map is onto. Its kernel contains $N_{L/K} C_L$, and the index equality for cyclic layers, by induction along a chain of cyclic subextensions, makes the kernel equal to it.

concepts.c:abelian-extension: Only abelian extensions are described by idele class groups.
concepts.c:galois-group: The Galois group is the target of the reciprocity isomorphism.
concepts.c:idele-class-group: The idele class group is the source whose norm quotient matches $G$.
concepts.c:artin-map: The Artin map is the homomorphism that the proof shows is an isomorphism.
concepts.c:frobenius-element: Frobenius elements fix the map at unramified primes.
concepts.c:norm-map: Norms from $L$ form the kernel of the reciprocity map.
concepts.c:local-field: Local class field theory at each completion supplies the local maps.

source.ref: J. Neukirch, Algebraic Number Theory, Grundlehren der mathematischen Wissenschaften 322, Springer, Berlin, 1999, chapters V and VI
source.note: Neukirch proves local class field theory (chapter V), the Herbrand quotient of the idele class group, the class field axiom and the global reciprocity law (chapter VI); E. Artin first proved the law in 1927.

statement: For a [normed space](c:normed-space) $E$ over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, the closed [unit ball](c:unit-ball) $\{\varphi \in E^* : \|\varphi\| \le 1\}$ of the [dual space](c:dual-space) $E^*$ is [compact](c:compact-space) in the [weak-* topology](c:weak-topology-2).

hypotheses.text: The space $E$ is a [normed space](c:normed-space) over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$.

conclusion: The set $\{\varphi \in E^* : \|\varphi\| \le 1\}$ is compact for the topology of pointwise convergence on $E$.

formal.difference: The declaration proves weak-* compactness of the polar of any neighborhood of $0$, over any nontrivially normed field that is a proper space. The closed unit ball is the polar of the unit ball of $E$ (WeakDual.isCompact_closedBall).

proofs.name: Embedding into a product of discs
proofs.slogan: Embed the dual ball into a product of compact discs by evaluation, show that its image is closed, and apply Tychonoff's theorem.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; for $E = 0$ the ball is one point.

roles.why: The norm bounds each value $|\varphi(x)| \le \|x\|$, and the scalar field has compact discs.

steps.slogan: Embed $E^*$ into the product $\prod_{x \in E} \mathbb{K}$ by evaluation at every point.
steps.detail: Send $\varphi$ to $(\varphi(x))_{x \in E}$. This map is injective, and the [weak-* topology](c:weak-topology-2) is by definition the topology it induces from the [product topology](c:product-topology). So it is a homeomorphism onto its image.

steps.slogan: Place the image of the ball inside the product of closed discs $D_x$ of radius $\|x\|$.
steps.detail: If $\|\varphi\| \le 1$, then $|\varphi(x)| \le \|x\|$ for every $x$, so the image lies in $P = \prod_x D_x$. Each closed disc $D_x$ in $\mathbb{K}$ is compact by the Heine–Borel theorem.

steps.slogan: Show that the product $P$ of compact discs is compact.
steps.detail: Tychonoff's theorem states that every product of compact spaces is [compact](c:compact-space) in the product topology. So $P$ is compact.

steps.slogan: Show that the image of the ball is a closed subset of $P$.
steps.detail: The image is the set of points $(t_x)$ of $P$ with $t_{x+y} = t_x + t_y$ and $t_{\lambda x} = \lambda t_x$ for all $x, y, \lambda$. Each condition is closed because coordinates are continuous, and such a point is a [linear functional](c:linear-functional) with $|t_x| \le \|x\|$, so it lies in the ball.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the ball is compact as a closed subset of a compact set.
steps.detail: A closed subset of the compact space $P$ is compact, so the image of the ball is compact. The homeomorphism of step 1 carries this back to the ball with the weak-* topology.

concepts.c:normed-space: The norm gives the bound $|\varphi(x)| \le \|x\|$ on the ball.
concepts.c:unit-ball: The dual unit ball is the set shown compact.
concepts.c:dual-space: The dual space consists of the bounded linear functionals on $E$.
concepts.c:compact-space: Compactness passes from the product of discs to the closed image.
concepts.c:weak-topology-2: The weak-* topology is the pointwise topology that the embedding induces.
concepts.c:product-topology: Tychonoff's theorem is a statement about the product topology.
concepts.c:linear-functional: Pointwise limits of linear functionals stay linear.

source.note: mathlib shows that the polar is bounded (isBounded_polar) and weak-* closed (isClosed_polar) and applies WeakDual.isCompact_of_bounded_of_closed, which uses Tychonoff's theorem (isCompact_pi_infinite).

statement: If $f\colon [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) and $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ have opposite signs, then $f(c) = 0$ for some $c$ in the open interval $(a, b)$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) on the [closed interval](c:closed-interval) $[a, b]$.
The end values have opposite signs: $f(a) f(b) < 0$.

proofs.name: Bisection
proofs.slogan: Halve the interval again and again, keep the half whose ends have opposite signs, and take the common point.
proofs.scope: The case $f(a) < 0 < f(b)$; the other case follows when the proof is applied to $-f$. If a midpoint is a zero, the process stops there.

roles.why: Continuity at the common point passes the signs of $f(a_k)$ and $f(b_k)$ to $f(c)$.
Opposite signs at the ends start the bisection and keep $c$ away from $a$ and $b$.

steps.slogan: Build nested intervals $[a_k, b_k]$ with $f(a_k) < 0 < f(b_k)$ by halving.
steps.detail: Start with $[a_0, b_0] = [a, b]$. If $m$ is the midpoint of $[a_k, b_k]$ and $f(m) \neq 0$, keep $[m, b_k]$ when $f(m) < 0$ and $[a_k, m]$ when $f(m) > 0$. The new interval has half the length and ends of opposite signs.

steps.slogan: Take the common [limit](c:limit-of-a-sequence) $c$ of the two monotone end sequences.
steps.detail: The sequence $a_k$ increases and $b_k$ decreases, and both are bounded by $a$ and $b$. Completeness of the [real numbers](c:real-number) gives limits, and $b_k - a_k = (b - a)/2^k \to 0$, so both converge to one point $c \in [a, b]$.

steps.slogan: Pass the signs to the limit to get $f(c) = 0$ with $a < c < b$.
steps.detail: Continuity gives $f(c) = \lim f(a_k) \le 0$ and $f(c) = \lim f(b_k) \ge 0$, so $f(c) = 0$. Since $f(a) \neq 0$ and $f(b) \neq 0$, the point $c$ is neither $a$ nor $b$.

concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity at $c$ turns limits of signs into the value $0$.
concepts.c:closed-interval: The closed interval holds the nested intervals and their limit point.
concepts.c:limit-of-a-sequence: The two end sequences converge to the same point $c$.
concepts.c:real-number: Completeness of the reals gives the limits of the monotone sequences.

source.note: The classical bisection proof, in the spirit of Bolzano's 1817 argument; see M. Spivak, Calculus, chapter 7.

statement: For the [stable unitary group](c:stable-unitary-group) $U$ and the [stable orthogonal group](c:stable-orthogonal-group) $O$, the [homotopy groups](c:homotopy-group) satisfy $\pi_k(U) \cong \pi_{k+2}(U)$ and $\pi_k(O) \cong \pi_{k+8}(O)$. Here $\pi_k(U)$ is $\mathbb{Z}$ for odd $k$ and $0$ for even $k$, and $\pi_0(O), \dots, \pi_7(O)$ are $\mathbb{Z}/2, \mathbb{Z}/2, 0, \mathbb{Z}, 0, 0, 0, \mathbb{Z}$.
conclusion: $\Omega U \simeq \mathbb{Z} \times BU$ and $\Omega^8 O \simeq O$, so the homotopy groups of $U$ have period $2$ and those of $O$ have period $8$, with the listed values.

proofs.name: Morse theory on spaces of geodesics
proofs.slogan: Identify the minimal geodesics in a classical group with a symmetric space, show that all other geodesics have large index, and read off loop spaces by Morse theory.
proofs.scope: An outline of Bott's proof; steps 2, 3 and 5 rest on the computations of the cited paper. The stable groups equal $\pi_k(U(n))$ for $2n > k$ and $\pi_k(O(n))$ for $n > k + 1$.

steps.slogan: Identify the minimal [geodesics](c:geodesic) from $I$ to $-I$ in $SU(2m)$ with a complex [Grassmannian](c:grassmannian).
steps.detail: For the bi-invariant metric, geodesics from $I$ are $t \mapsto \exp(tA)$. Those of minimal length from $I$ to $-I$ correspond to the $m$-dimensional complex subspaces of $\mathbb{C}^{2m}$, the eigenspaces of $A$, so they form $G_m(\mathbb{C}^{2m})$.

steps.slogan: Compute the Morse indices of the other geodesics from the curvature of the group.
steps.detail: The Morse index theorem counts conjugate points along each geodesic through the curvature operator of the symmetric metric. Bott shows that every nonminimal geodesic from $I$ to $-I$ has index at least $2m + 2$.

steps.slogan: Compare the space of paths from $I$ to $-I$ with the space of minimal geodesics.
steps.detail: Morse theory for the energy shows that this path space, which is homotopy equivalent to the [loop space](c:loop-space) $\Omega SU(2m)$, is the minimal-geodesic space with cells of dimension at least $2m + 2$ attached. Hence $\pi_i(G_m(\mathbb{C}^{2m})) \cong \pi_{i+1}(SU(2m))$ for $i \le 2m$.

steps.slogan: Let $m$ grow to get $\Omega U \simeq \mathbb{Z} \times BU$ and the period two.
steps.detail: As $m \to \infty$ the Grassmannians give $BU$, and $\pi_i(BU) \cong \pi_{i-1}(U)$. So $\pi_{i+1}(U) \cong \pi_i(BU) \cong \pi_{i-1}(U)$ for $i \ge 1$.

steps.slogan: Iterate the geodesic argument through eight symmetric spaces for the orthogonal group.
steps.detail: Bott applies the same method to the chain $O$, $O/U$, $U/Sp$, $\mathbb{Z} \times BSp$, $Sp$, $Sp/U$, $U/O$, $\mathbb{Z} \times BO$ of [symmetric spaces](c:symmetric-space). Each one is stably the space of minimal geodesics in the loop space of the previous one, so $\Omega^8 O \simeq O$.

steps.slogan: Read off all groups from the periods and the low-dimensional groups.
steps.detail: For $U$: $\pi_0(U) = 0$ because $U(n)$ is connected, and $\pi_1(U) = \mathbb{Z}$ through the determinant. For $O$: the eight loop-space identifications give $\pi_k(O) \cong \pi_0$ of the $(k+1)$-th space of the chain, which yields $\mathbb{Z}/2, \mathbb{Z}/2, 0, \mathbb{Z}, 0, 0, 0, \mathbb{Z}$.

concepts.c:stable-unitary-group: Its homotopy groups have period two.
concepts.c:stable-orthogonal-group: Its homotopy groups have period eight.
concepts.c:homotopy-group: The theorem computes all homotopy groups of the stable classical groups.
concepts.c:geodesic: Minimal geodesics form the space that approximates the loop space.
concepts.c:grassmannian: The Grassmannian is the space of minimal geodesics in $SU(2m)$.
concepts.c:loop-space: Periodicity is a homotopy equivalence between iterated loop spaces.
concepts.c:symmetric-space: Each stage of the real chain is a symmetric space of minimal geodesics.

source.ref: R. Bott, The stable homotopy of the classical groups, Annals of Mathematics 70 (1959), 313-337
source.note: Bott identifies the minimal geodesics, computes the indices of the others and applies Morse theory to the loop spaces; J. Milnor, Morse Theory (1963), part IV, gives the same proof.

statement: Every [continuous](c:continuous-function) map $f\colon K \to K$ from a nonempty [compact](c:compact-space) [convex set](c:convex-set) $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ to itself has a [fixed point](c:fixed-point).

hypotheses.text: The set $K$ is nonempty.
The set $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is [compact](c:compact-space).
The set $K$ is [convex](c:convex-set).
The map $f\colon K \to K$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function).

proofs.name: No retraction by homology
proofs.slogan: Reduce to the ball, turn a map without fixed points into a retraction onto the sphere, and contradict the homology of the sphere.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for $n \ge 1$; for $n = 0$ the set $K$ is one point, which is fixed.

roles.why: A nonempty $K$ has nearest points, so the retraction $p$ is defined.
Compactness gives the nearest points and a ball that contains $K$.
Convexity makes the nearest point unique and the map $p$ continuous.
Continuity of $f$ makes the ray map $r$ continuous.

steps.slogan: Retract a closed ball onto $K$ by the nearest-point map and reduce to the ball.
steps.detail: Choose a closed [ball](c:ball) $B \supseteq K$, and let $p(y)$ be the nearest point of $K$ to $y$, which exists because $K$ is compact and nonempty and is unique because $K$ is [convex](c:convex-set). The map $p$ is continuous and fixes $K$, so a fixed point $x$ of $f \circ p\colon B \to B$ lies in $K$ and satisfies $f(x) = x$.

steps.slogan: Assume that $g\colon D^n \to D^n$ has no fixed point and push each point along a ray to the sphere.
steps.detail: Let $r(x)$ be the point where the ray from $g(x)$ through $x$ meets the [sphere](c:sphere) $S^{n-1}$. It solves a quadratic equation with a positive root that depends continuously on $x$, and $r(x) = x$ for $x \in S^{n-1}$, so $r$ is a retraction of $D^n$ onto $S^{n-1}$.

steps.slogan: Apply reduced homology to the retraction and the inclusion of the sphere.
steps.detail: From $r \circ i = \mathrm{id}$ we get $r_* i_* = \mathrm{id}$ on $\tilde H_{n-1}(S^{n-1}) \cong \mathbb{Z}$, computed by excision. But $i_*$ factors through $\tilde H_{n-1}(D^n) = 0$ because the ball is contractible, so $\mathbb{Z} = 0$, a contradiction.

concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity of $f$ passes to the retraction built from it.
concepts.c:compact-space: Compactness gives nearest points and a bounding ball.
concepts.c:convex-set: Convexity makes the nearest-point map a continuous retraction.
concepts.c:fixed-point: The theorem asserts the existence of a fixed point.
concepts.c:ball: The closed ball is the model domain after the reduction.
concepts.c:sphere: The boundary sphere would be a retract if no fixed point existed.
concepts.c:homology: Homology distinguishes the sphere from the contractible ball.

source.note: The standard homological proof, as in A. Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, corollary 2.15.

proofs.name: Smooth case by Sard and approximation
proofs.slogan: Rule out smooth retractions onto the sphere by Sard's theorem, then pass from smooth maps to continuous maps by uniform approximation.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for $n \ge 1$, after the reduction to the ball; for $n = 0$ the set $K$ is one point.

roles.why: A nonempty $K$ has nearest points, so the retraction $p$ is defined.
Compactness gives nearest points, and on the ball it gives a positive minimum of $|g(x) - x|$.
Convexity makes the nearest point unique and the map $p$ continuous.
A continuous map is a uniform limit of polynomial maps on the ball.

steps.slogan: Retract a closed ball onto $K$ by the nearest-point map and reduce to the ball.
steps.detail: Choose a closed [ball](c:ball) $B \supseteq K$, and let $p(y)$ be the nearest point of $K$ to $y$, which exists because $K$ is compact and nonempty and is unique because $K$ is [convex](c:convex-set). The map $p$ is continuous and fixes $K$, so a fixed point $x$ of $f \circ p\colon B \to B$ lies in $K$ and satisfies $f(x) = x$.

steps.slogan: Rule out a smooth retraction $D^n \to S^{n-1}$ by a regular value of Sard's theorem.
steps.detail: Sard's theorem gives a [regular value](c:regular-value) $y \in S^{n-1}$ of a smooth retraction $r$. Then $r^{-1}(y)$ is a compact one-dimensional manifold with boundary whose boundary is $r^{-1}(y) \cap S^{n-1} = \{y\}$. A compact one-manifold has an even number of boundary points, a contradiction.

steps.slogan: Show that every [smooth map](c:smooth-map) $D^n \to D^n$ has a fixed point.
steps.detail: If a smooth $g$ had no fixed point, the ray from $g(x)$ through $x$ would meet $S^{n-1}$ at a point that depends smoothly on $x$. This gives a smooth retraction, which step 2 excludes.

steps.slogan: Approximate a continuous map without fixed points by a smooth map without fixed points.
steps.detail: If continuous $g$ has no fixed point, compactness gives $\mu > 0$ with $|g(x) - x| \ge \mu$. Stone–Weierstrass gives a polynomial map $P$ with $|P - g| < \mu/2$, and $P_1 = P/(1 + \mu/2)$ maps $D^n$ into itself with $|P_1 - g| < \mu$, so $P_1$ has no fixed point, against step 3.

concepts.c:continuous-function: The continuous map is approximated by smooth maps.
concepts.c:compact-space: Compactness gives nearest points and a positive minimum distance.
concepts.c:convex-set: Convexity makes the nearest-point map a continuous retraction.
concepts.c:fixed-point: The theorem asserts the existence of a fixed point.
concepts.c:ball: The closed ball is the model domain after the reduction.
concepts.c:regular-value: A regular value makes its preimage a one-dimensional manifold.
concepts.c:smooth-map: Sard's theorem needs smooth maps, so the proof first treats them.

statement: Every [orthogonal transformation](c:orthogonal-transformation) of a real [inner product space](c:inner-product-space) of finite dimension $n$ is a composition of at most $n$ [reflections](c:reflection-at-a-hyperplane) in hyperplanes.

hypotheses.text: The space $V$ is a real [inner product space](c:inner-product-space) of finite dimension $n$.
The map $\varphi\colon V \to V$ is an [orthogonal transformation](c:orthogonal-transformation): a linear bijection that preserves inner products.

conclusion: $\varphi = \rho_1 \cdots \rho_k$ for some reflections $\rho_i$ in hyperplanes, with $k \le n$.

proofs.name: Induction on the moved part
proofs.slogan: Reflect one moved vector back to its image, which enlarges the fixed subspace, and induct on the dimension of its orthogonal complement.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; the identity is the empty composition. For general nondegenerate symmetric bilinear forms the theorem also holds, but isotropic vectors need an extra argument that this proof does not give.

roles.why: Finite dimension bounds $\dim W^\perp$ by $n$ and lets the induction stop.
Preserving inner products keeps $W^\perp$ invariant and gives $\|v\| = \|\varphi v\|$.

steps.slogan: Let $W$ be the fixed subspace of $\varphi$ and induct on $k = \dim W^\perp$.
steps.detail: Set $W = \ker(\mathrm{id} - \varphi)$ and claim that $\varphi$ is a product of at most $k$ reflections; since $k \le n$, this proves the theorem. If $k = 0$, then $W = V$ and $\varphi$ is the identity, the empty product.

steps.slogan: Pick a nonzero $v \in W^\perp$ and show that $\varphi v \in W^\perp$ and $\varphi v \neq v$.
steps.detail: For $w \in W$, $\langle \varphi v, w \rangle = \langle \varphi v, \varphi w \rangle = \langle v, w \rangle = 0$, so $\varphi v \in W^\perp$. Since $v \notin W$, $\varphi v \neq v$.

steps.slogan: Reflect in the [hyperplane](c:hyperplane) orthogonal to $x = v - \varphi v$ to swap $v$ and $\varphi v$.
steps.detail: Let $\rho(y) = y - 2\langle y, x \rangle x/\langle x, x \rangle$. Since $\|v\| = \|\varphi v\|$, $\langle v + \varphi v, x \rangle = 0$, so $\rho$ fixes $v + \varphi v$ and negates $x$, which gives $\rho(\varphi v) = v$. Since $x \in W^\perp$, $\rho$ fixes $W$ pointwise.

steps.slogan: Show that the fixed subspace of $\rho\varphi$ contains $W$ and $v$.
steps.detail: For $w \in W$, $\rho\varphi w = \rho w = w$, and $\rho\varphi v = v$. So the fixed subspace $W'$ of $\rho\varphi$ contains $W + \mathbb{R}v$, which is larger than $W$, and $\dim W'^\perp \le k - 1$.

steps.slogan: Write $\varphi = \rho(\rho\varphi)$ and apply the induction hypothesis to $\rho\varphi$.
steps.detail: By induction, $\rho\varphi$ is a product of at most $k - 1$ reflections. Since $\rho^2 = \mathrm{id}$, $\varphi = \rho(\rho\varphi)$ is a product of at most $k \le n$ reflections.

concepts.c:orthogonal-transformation: The map preserves inner products, so it keeps $W^\perp$ invariant.
concepts.c:inner-product-space: The inner product defines orthogonal complements and reflections.
concepts.c:reflection-at-a-hyperplane: Each induction step peels off one reflection.
concepts.c:hyperplane: The reflection fixes the hyperplane orthogonal to $v - \varphi v$.

statement: For a [power series](c:power-series) $\sum a_n (z - c)^n$ with complex coefficients, the [radius of convergence](c:radius-of-convergence) $R$ satisfies $1/R = \limsup_{n \to \infty} |a_n|^{1/n}$, with $1/0 = \infty$ and $1/\infty = 0$. The series converges absolutely for $|z - c| < R$ and diverges for $|z - c| > R$.

hypotheses.text: The coefficients $a_n$ and the center $c$ are complex numbers.

conclusion: $R = 1/\limsup |a_n|^{1/n}$, and $R$ separates absolute convergence from divergence.

formal.difference: The declaration is stated for formal multilinear series between normed spaces, with $\|p_n\|$ in place of $|a_n|$ and the radius defined by boundedness of $\|p_n\| r^n$. It does not itself state convergence inside and divergence outside.

proofs.name: Comparison of $r^n |a_n|$ with $1$
proofs.slogan: Define the radius by boundedness of $|a_n| r^n$, rewrite $|a_n| r^n \le 1$ as a root bound, and compare both sides as $n \to \infty$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, including $R = 0$ and $R = \infty$ through the conventions on $1/0$ and $1/\infty$.

roles.why: The absolute values $|a_n|$ and $|z - c|$ make the comparison with geometric series possible.

steps.slogan: Define $R$ as the supremum of the $r \ge 0$ with $|a_n| r^n$ bounded, and relate it to convergence.
steps.detail: If $|a_n| r^n \le C$ and $|z - c| < r$, then $|a_n (z - c)^n| \le C q^n$ with $q = |z - c|/r < 1$, so the series has [absolute convergence](c:absolute-convergence) by comparison with a [geometric series](c:geometric-series). If $|z - c| > R$, the terms are unbounded and the series diverges.

steps.slogan: Rewrite the bound $|a_n| r^n \le 1$ as $r \le |a_n|^{-1/n}$ for $n \ge 1$.
steps.detail: Taking $n$-th roots keeps the order of nonnegative numbers, so $|a_n| r^n \le 1$ holds exactly when $r |a_n|^{1/n} \le 1$, that is, $r \le 1/|a_n|^{1/n}$ with $1/0 = \infty$.

steps.slogan: Show that every $r < R$ satisfies $r \le \liminf |a_n|^{-1/n}$.
steps.detail: Choose $r < r' < R$ with $|a_n| r'^n \le C$. Then $|a_n| r^n \le C (r/r')^n \to 0$, so $|a_n| r^n \le 1$ for large $n$, and step 2 gives $r \le |a_n|^{-1/n}$ for large $n$. Hence $r$ is at most the [limit inferior](c:limit-inferior).

steps.slogan: Show that every $r < \liminf |a_n|^{-1/n}$ satisfies $r \le R$.
steps.detail: For large $n$, $r < |a_n|^{-1/n}$, so $|a_n| r^n \le 1$ by step 2. The finitely many other terms are bounded too, so $|a_n| r^n$ is bounded and $r \le R$.

steps.slogan: Combine both bounds and invert to get $1/R = \limsup |a_n|^{1/n}$.
steps.detail: Steps 3 and 4 give $R = \liminf |a_n|^{-1/n}$. The map $t \mapsto 1/t$ reverses order on $[0, \infty]$ and turns the limit inferior into the [limit superior](c:limit-superior), so $1/R = \limsup |a_n|^{1/n}$; with step 1 this $R$ is the radius of convergence.

concepts.c:power-series: The theorem computes the radius of a power series from its coefficients.
concepts.c:radius-of-convergence: The radius is defined by bounded terms and then computed.
concepts.c:limit-superior: The formula expresses $1/R$ as a limit superior of roots.
concepts.c:limit-inferior: The radius itself is a limit inferior of inverse roots.
concepts.c:absolute-convergence: Inside the radius the series converges absolutely.
concepts.c:geometric-series: Comparison with a geometric series gives convergence inside the radius.
